notes: \cpara{The essay's evidence base, declared in its first sentence: the author does not ask, and so does not know. Everything that follows about how rationalists grow rests on stories that some acquaintances chose to volunteer. The essay admits this and then, three paragraphs later, states a universal law.}

\cpara{A selection effect presented as a finding. People whose family joined a cult have a story to volunteer; people with ordinary childhoods do not. ``Surprising tendency'' has no base rate to be surprising against. ``Reaching upward as rationalists'' is the author's private ranking of acquaintances.}
\cpara{The author's own childhood is placed in the same class as a cult and a psychotic parent, then called ``tame.''}

\cpara{The thesis, stated as a law (``you don't start growing'') right after the admission that the author does not know the trend. The next sentence concedes not knowing why it holds, and the two ``maybe'' explanations are guesses. A claim with no evidence and no mechanism is offered as the gate to the reader's development.}
\cpara{Offers another guess: perhaps you do not work hard at being unusually sane unless ordinary people frighten you.}

\cpara{Here the essay shows what the broken trust is for. The ``strange ideas'' are cryonics and many-worlds, two positions the author holds. A reader who hesitates is described as someone who can ``see the logic'' and is held back only by the people around them. That the logic might be wrong is not among the options. Doubt about the author's views is recast as a symptom of social dependence.}
\cpara{Answers yes, the crowd can be wrong, pointing to corn ethanol and environmentalists opposing nuclear power.}

\cpara{The obvious objection, that telling people to break with those around them and trust a new group is how cults recruit, is answered with a link to the author's own post on the subject. The parenthesis then labels the reader's unease (``nervously seeking reassurance'') as the thing to overcome. The warning sign is reclassified as the obstacle.}

\cpara{Flattery for the reader who has broken with family and friends: such people judge ideas ``on their merits.'' No evidence is given that they do. The author's earlier post says the opposite: ``You wouldn't want to end up as a free thinker. It's not a \emph{virtue}, you see---just a bias either way'' (``Lonely Dissent,'' 2007). ``Hopefully forward'' concedes that nothing in this state points anywhere in particular.}

\cpara{A pointer to the earlier post, whose central caution is left behind. That post said: ``Other people do have reasons for thinking what they do, and ignoring that completely is as bad as being afraid to contradict them.'' This essay keeps the clown suit and drops the caution.}
\cpara{Gives an example of such dissent: telling confident election forecasters to bet on a prediction market, while others merely admire independent thinking.}
\cpara{The law returns as the author's personal observation: ``I've never seen anyone.'' That is the filtered sample of the second paragraph again, now stated as a universal.}
\cpara{Says things might differ elsewhere, and doubts that people can trust and think at once.}

\cpara{This paragraph and the next make one point: Eliezer18 blamed the people, not the ideal. It is an accurate description of how any ideal is defended, including the ideal of ``Bayescraft'' later in this essay. It is not applied there.}
\cpara{Explains that blaming people for falling short lets you avoid questioning the ideal.}
\cpara{Asks who would question that experiment decides between hypotheses.}

\cpara{Everyone who questioned Science was ``without exception'' on ``the Dark Side.'' This is the younger self speaking, and the paragraph's first sentence corrects it (``an aversion to ideas that resembled things idiots had said''). But it names no serious critic of scientific method: Kuhn, Lakatos and Feyerabend, whose \textsc{Against Method} appeared in 1975, go unmentioned.}

\cpara{The claim that Science could be questioned only in order to be accepted describes the author's teenage reading, not the state of thought about science. ``The master idea, the idea that let you change ideas'' is the author's own gloss, presented as what everyone believed.}

\cpara{The story from ``When Science Can't Help,'' three days earlier, told again. ``Professed that I wished to test'' is exact: the idea was professed testable, and nothing in either post says it was tested.}
\cpara{Says the author therefore felt safe, like a child who has obeyed every rule of a trusted parent.}

\cpara{The turning point of the story sits uneasily with the author's earlier account. In 2007 the author wrote: ``Beyond a doubt, my allegiance to Traditional Rationality helped me get out of the hole I dug myself into,'' though it ``still wasn't enough to get it \emph{right}.'' Here, ``Traditional Rationality had not saved him.'' The two fit if ``saved'' means ``prevented,'' but the essay does not mention the help.}
\cpara{Describes the author's reaction: no great upheaval, just a plain sense of having been stupid.}

\cpara{The purpose, stated plainly: to break the reader's trust in the method they already have. The rest of the essay says that Bayescraft will not make the reader safe either, but it does supply the author's reading list.}
\cpara{Claims Science cannot save you: its ideals predate probability theory and bias research, and it asks too little and tolerates slowness.}
\cpara{Warns that following the rules of Science does not make your reasoning defensible.}

\cpara{Turn it on the author. If no procedure makes reasoning defensible, none makes the author's reasoning about many-worlds defensible. A week earlier the verdict was that many-worlds ``\emph{wins outright} given our current state of evidence'' and ``\emph{is} an obvious fact, if you have all your marbles lined up correctly'' (``Many Worlds, One Best Guess''). The warning that you are never safe is for the reader's beliefs, not the author's.}
\cpara{Claims no known set of rules guarantees you will not be a fool.}
\cpara{Claims no known ethics of reasoning protects you from criticism if you obey it.}
\cpara{Adds that Bayesian reasoning is no exception: it is harder, and you cannot be sure you do it right.}

\cpara{Overstated by the author's own earlier account. In 2007 the author described switching ``to Bayescraft (Laplace / Jaynes / Tversky / Kahneman)'' (``The Importance of Saying Oops''). Jaynes, whom the author called ``a late grand master of the Bayesian Conspiracy'' two months earlier, left a textbook, \textsc{Probability Theory: The Logic of Science} (2003). ``No textbooks, no elderly mentors'' erases the sources the author names elsewhere, though the sentence's end narrows the claim: what is missing is how to apply the knowledge ``to the case of correcting yourself.''}
\cpara{Warns that you do not know what your mind is doing, and cannot tell whether you have corrected for a bias.}

\cpara{``Impossible to apply'' contradicts the author's case for many-worlds, five days earlier, which applied it: ``you could write the two hypotheses out as computer programs and count the lines of code'' (``The Dilemma: Science or Bayes?''). Either the math cannot be applied or it settles many-worlds. The essay uses the first claim on the reader and the second for the author. ``John Q. Unbeliever'' is a strawman with a name.}
\cpara{Argues that Science is too vague to frighten you, since testing ideas by experiment seems impossible to get wrong.}
\cpara{Contrasts probability theory: seeing math you cannot actually apply makes clear the task is hard and you may be failing.}
\cpara{The conclusion of the litany, in four words. It does not follow from the premises. That every method can fail does not mean that no method can be relied on more than another.}
\cpara{Predicts that these words will not break your trust; only a disaster from following the rules will.}
\cpara{Says the author's younger self already believed Science could be questioned, as good rationalists question everything.}
\cpara{Explains what Eliezer18 did not believe: that following Science could really lead to failure.}
\cpara{Adds that Eliezer18 said failure was possible, as a formula.}
\cpara{Says Eliezer18 did not expect real failure: flaws were to be sought, not found.}
\cpara{Admits this change of feeling is hard to convey, and fears no warning can do it.}

\cpara{The prescription: take ``all that you have learned here'' as far as it goes, and find that ``this too fails you.'' The essay includes its own teachings among the things that will fail, but it does not say what the reader should conclude about them when they do.}
\cpara{``Something to protect'' is a term from an earlier post, undefined here.}

\cpara{``Sole responsibility,'' no ``trustworthy defenses,'' a ``higher Art'': the reward for losing trust in everything is to ``start your journey as a rationalist.'' What is promised is an identity and a path, not a method the reader can check.}
\cpara{The claim is unfalsifiable: anyone who seems to search without such losses has not ``truly'' begun.}

\cpara{The essay claims to contain a flaw that ``affects one of the conclusions'' and does not say which. The device comes from Kai Chang's post ``My Favorite Liar'' (February 2008), about a teacher who told his class that ``it is my intention to work into each of my lectures \ldots\ one lie.'' In the 75 comments on the post that I retrieved, the author does not identify the flaw.}

\cpara{The second half of the device. Any flaw a reader finds may be the planted one, and any flaw the reader insists on may be ``a flaw that is not a real flaw.'' Real flaws still count, but the reader is given no way to tell which kind they have found.}

\cpara{``There are flaws, they are serious and you have not found them'': a certainty about flaws no one has seen. It cannot be checked, and it is the one thing the essay asks the reader to know ``on a gut level.''}
